extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism researchers, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy and guidance for identifying the news values that make stories likely to be selected and published (including contemporary factors such as social-media shareability and audio-visual appeal). Intended for analysing or making editorial selection decisions across newspapers and digital/social platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories generated by, or available first to, the news organisation as a result of interviews, letters, investigations, surveys, polls, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being first or having original material increases newsworthiness; exclusives derive from unique access or original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly negative overtones such as death, injury, defeat and loss (of a job, for example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative outcomes often attract attention and selection; 'bad news' remains a strong and frequent news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning conflict such as controversies, arguments, splits, strikes, fights, insurrections and warfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict-driven narratives (disagreements, battles, disputes) are inherently newsworthy because they dramatise opposition and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that have an element of surprise, contrast and/or the unusual about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected or counter-intuitive elements make stories stand out; surprise can be used as the 'peg' for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio-visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that have arresting photographs, video, audio and/or which can be illustrated with infographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong visuals or multimedia formats increase appeal, particularly online and on social platforms; visual-led items often score highly for shareability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are thought likely to generate sharing and comments via Facebook, Twitter and other forms of social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareability is an emergent contemporary news value; qualities that promote sharing are hard to define but include emotional triggers (e.g., 'stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry'), strong visuals, or easily digestible formats. Newsrooms may prioritise shareability due to traffic/click incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft stories concerning sex, showbusiness, sport, lighter human interest, animals, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, witty headlines or lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entertainment content is highly popular on social media and can dominate selection when publishers prioritise accessible, fun, or amusing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning an unfolding drama such as escapes, accidents, searches, sieges, rescues, battles or court cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing or unfolding dramatic events sustain audience attention and are likely to be selected for repeated coverage and updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about subjects already in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing coverage of existing stories (updates, developments, new angles) is a distinct value that justifies further selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power elite
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organisations, institutions or corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions and actions of elites are traditionally newsworthy because of their influence and decision-making consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about groups or nations perceived to be influential with, or culturally or historically familiar to, the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience familiarity and perceived influence determine whether an event or issue resonates; relevance is audience- and context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories perceived as sufficiently significant in the large numbers of people involved or in potential impact, or involving a degree of extreme behaviour or extreme occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale, scope, or extremity (many people affected, large impact, unusually extreme events) increases newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning people who are already famous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fame itself confers news value; celebrity stories often attract attention even when intrinsic significance is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly positive overtones such as recoveries, breakthroughs, cures, wins and celebrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive developments and optimistic outcomes constitute a distinct news value that can balance the prevalence of negative stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: News organisation’s agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that set or fit the news organisation’s own agenda, whether ideological, commercial or as part of a specific campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial priorities, ideological stances, commercial goals or campaign strategies shape selection; agenda alignment can elevate otherwise marginal items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and practical constraints on selection
rubrics_metrics.description: News values are contested and mediated by practical considerations (availability of resources and time) and subjective, often unconscious influences (social, educational, ideological and cultural influences on journalists), workplace position, audience type, medium, and who is selecting the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the taxonomy as an analytic tool rather than a deterministic checklist: similar events may receive different prominence depending on resources, medium (print vs social), editorial roles, and pressures (e.g., online clicks/shares). Recognise that selection decisions mix intrinsic news values with situational constraints and incentives.
